The United States responded by creating [NASA] in 1958. In 1961, President Kennedy announced an incredible goal: to send a man to the Moon before the end of the decade!

The Cold War also led to real wars in other places, like Korea and Vietnam. It ended in 1989 with the fall of the Berlin Wall, and in 1991 the Soviet Union broke up.

title: Martin Luther King: "I have a dream"
text:
After the Montgomery bus boycott, the [civil rights] movement grew. Everywhere in the South, Black Americans and their white supporters protested peacefully against segregation.

In 1960, four Black students sat at a lunch counter reserved for white people in Greensboro, North Carolina, and asked to be served. They were refused, but came back every day, with more and more friends. These "sit-ins" spread to many cities.

In 1963, in Birmingham, Alabama, the police used dogs and powerful fire hoses against peaceful protesters, even children. The images, shown on television, shocked the whole country.

On the 28th of August 1963, about 250,000 people, Black and white, gathered in Washington, D.C., in front of the Lincoln Memorial. It was the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, one of the largest demonstrations in American history.

Martin Luther King Jr. gave a speech that became world-famous. He said:
"I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character."

He dreamed that one day, Black and white children would hold hands like brothers and sisters.

His words touched millions of people. In 1964, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act, which banned segregation in public places and [discrimination] at work. In 1965, the Voting Rights Act protected the right of Black Americans to vote.

The same year, Martin Luther King received the Nobel Peace Prize, at the age of 35.

But the struggle was dangerous. On the 4th of April 1968, Martin Luther King was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee. He was 39 years old.

Today, the third Monday of January is a national holiday in his honour, Martin Luther King Jr. Day. His dream still inspires people around the world.

title: Apollo 11: men walk on the Moon
text:
In 1961, President Kennedy promised that the United States would send a man to the Moon and bring him back safely before 1970. It seemed impossible! At that time, the Americans had only sent one astronaut into space, for 15 minutes.

To succeed, NASA launched the Apollo programme. About 400,000 people worked on it: engineers, scientists, technicians, seamstresses who sewed the spacesuits... Brilliant mathematicians, like Katherine Johnson, an African American woman, calculated the trajectories.

Engineers built the most powerful [rocket] ever made: Saturn V. It was 110 metres tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty!

On the 16th of July 1969, Apollo 11 took off from Florida with three astronauts: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins. The journey to the Moon took about four days.

On the 20th of July 1969, Armstrong and Aldrin climbed into the small lunar module, called the Eagle, and descended towards the Moon, while Collins stayed in orbit. The computer showed alarms, and the planned landing site was full of rocks. Armstrong had to take control and fly further. When he landed, there were only a few seconds of fuel left! He announced: "The Eagle has landed."

A few hours later, Armstrong went down the ladder and put his foot on the Moon's dust. He said: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

About 600 million people around the world watched on television!

The two astronauts walked on the Moon for about two and a half hours. They collected rocks, planted an American flag and left a plaque saying: "We came in peace for all mankind." Their footprints are still there, because there is no wind on the Moon!

Between 1969 and 1972, twelve astronauts walked on the Moon. Today, NASA's Artemis programme wants to send humans back, including the first woman.

title: Computers for everyone and the internet
text:
In the 1950s and 1960s, computers were gigantic machines that filled whole rooms. They were very expensive and used only by governments, universities and big companies.

Then engineers invented the [microchip], a tiny piece of silicon capable of doing millions of calculations. Computers became smaller and smaller. In California, south of San Francisco, many technology companies set up. This region was nicknamed Silicon Valley.

In 1976, two young friends, Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, founded a company in a garage: Apple. Wozniak built the Apple I, then in 1977 the Apple II, one of the first personal computers sold to the general public, with a keyboard and colour graphics. It was a huge success!

At the same time, Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded Microsoft in 1975. They wrote the programs that made computers work. Their Windows software was later used on most computers in the world.

In 1981, IBM launched its "PC", personal computer. Soon, computers entered offices, schools and homes. Children played the first video games!

Meanwhile, the American army and universities had created a network to connect computers to each other, called ARPANET, in 1969. It was the ancestor of the [internet].

In 1989, a British scientist working in Switzerland, Tim Berners-Lee, invented the World Wide Web: web pages linked together that everyone could visit. In the 1990s, the internet spread across the world. People discovered e-mail, websites, and later search engines like Google, founded in 1998 by two students.

In 2007, Apple launched the iPhone, and smartphones put the internet in everyone's pocket.

Today, American technology companies are among the biggest in the world. Computers, the internet and [artificial intelligence] are changing the way we learn, work and communicate.

title: September 11, 2001
text:
On the morning of Tuesday the 11th of September 2001, the United States suffered the deadliest attack in its history.

Nineteen [terrorists] from a group called al-Qaeda took control of four passenger planes.

At 8:46 in the morning, the first plane crashed into the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York. These two twin towers, 110 floors high, were among the tallest buildings in the world. A few minutes later, a second plane hit the South Tower. The whole world watched on television, in shock. Less than two hours later, the two towers collapsed.

A third plane crashed into the Pentagon, the headquarters of the American army, near Washington.

On the fourth plane, passengers learned by phone what had happened. They decided to fight back against the hijackers. The plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. Their courage probably saved many lives, because the plane was heading for Washington.

Nearly 3,000 people were killed, from more than 90 countries. Among them were 343 New York [firefighters] who had rushed into the towers to save people.

In the days that followed, Americans showed great solidarity. People queued to give blood, and volunteers came from all over the country to help. Many countries expressed their support. The French newspaper Le Monde wrote: "We are all Americans."

The attacks changed the world. The United States launched a war in Afghanistan against al-Qaeda and the Taliban, then in 2003 a war in Iraq. Security was tightened everywhere, especially in airports.

Today, at the site of the towers in New York, there is a memorial: two large square pools, with waterfalls, in the place where the towers stood. The names of all the victims are engraved around them. Next to it stands a new tower, One World Trade Center, 541 metres (1,776 feet) tall, like the year of independence.

title: Barack Obama, the first Black president
text:
Barack Obama was born in 1961 in Honolulu, Hawaii. His mother was a white American from Kansas, and his father was a student from Kenya, in Africa. He spent part of his childhood in Indonesia, then was raised mainly by his grandparents in Hawaii.

He studied law at Harvard University, where he became the first Black president of the famous Harvard Law Review. Then he worked in Chicago helping poor neighbourhoods, and taught about the Constitution. In Chicago, he met Michelle Robinson, a lawyer, and they married in 1992. They have two daughters, Malia and Sasha.

He became a senator for Illinois, then in 2008, he ran for president. His slogan was "Yes, we can!" Many young people, who had never been interested in politics, supported him.

On the 4th of November 2008, Barack Obama was elected the 44th President of the United States. He was the first African American to become president! It was a very emotional moment for many people, especially for those who had fought for civil rights. Only about 45 years earlier, in some states, Black Americans could hardly vote.

On the 20th of January 2009, about 1.8 million people came to Washington to watch his inauguration. He swore the oath on the Bible that Abraham Lincoln had used.

He took office during a serious economic crisis. As president, he passed a law so that millions more Americans could have [health insurance]. He was re-elected in 2012, and served two terms, until 2017.

In 2009, he received the Nobel Peace Prize.

Michelle Obama, the [First Lady], encouraged children to eat healthily and do sport, and planted a vegetable garden at the White House.

His election showed that in the United States, things can change, even if the fight against racism is not over.

title: The United States today: 250 years
text:
On the 4th of July 2026, the United States celebrated its 250th birthday! Its semiquincentennial: 250 years since the Declaration of Independence.

The United States is a huge country: the third or fourth largest in the world. It is made up of 50 states, plus the capital, Washington, D.C. 48 states are next to each other, between Canada and Mexico, and two are far away: Alaska, near the Arctic, and Hawaii, in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. The flag, nicknamed the "Stars and Stripes", has 50 stars, one for each state, and 13 stripes for the 13 original colonies.

The country has about 340 million inhabitants, the third largest population in the world after India and China. It is a [federal] republic: each state has its own government and laws, but also shares a national government. The president is elected every four years and can serve only two terms. In 2025, Donald Trump began his second term as the 47th president.

The landscapes are incredibly varied: the skyscrapers of New York, the deserts of Arizona, the Grand Canyon, the Rocky Mountains, the Great Lakes, the beaches of Florida and California, the glaciers of Alaska, the volcanoes of Hawaii...

The United States is often called a "nation of immigrants". Apart from Native Americans, almost all Americans have ancestors who came from somewhere else, from Europe, Africa, Latin America, Asia... More than 350 languages are spoken in American homes!

American culture is known all over the world: Hollywood films, jazz, rock and roll, hip-hop, superheroes, baseball, basketball, hamburgers...

But the country also faces big challenges: inequality between rich and poor, the long fight against racism, [climate change], and deep disagreements between Americans about many questions.

The history of the United States continues to be written. What chapter would you like to add?
